She said, “I'm not a hundred percent certain, but I, I think I can offer seven-fifty, with maybe twenty percent down. The thing is, I've got some...research and they're going to buy it and usually they pay so much and they really like my work and I've got a meeting lined up and...well, I should know in the next couple days.”
“Alright,” I said, again at a loss for words. 
“We'll talk about it tomorrow,” she said. “Either on the phone or, I hope, over dinner.”
#
1. Unc threw a fit when I told him I wanted to go into the city while he was here inoculating the Fleet. 
“What do you mean you're going to the city?” He said. “You can't leave me here to run the inoculation alone. I don't care how many extra hands we hire, I can't lead them all on my own. We don't keep the Fleet in shape, we don't make our money, we don't fix up the property, we don't sell the property. You don't get it. It's important, son.”
“That's why I'm doing it, Unc. That's why I'm going. Because she wants to buy the farm and she wants to talk about it over dinner,” I yelled. “Don't make it about me and you. So yeah, I'm going.” 
“Bull. Shit. What kind of dinner lasts all day long, MacElray? This ain't about the ranch, or she'da made a for real offer already. And this sure in hell ain't about you and me, Mac. This is about you. Just you. So, fine. Fine! Go.” 
I pushed over the dewar and let its contents sizzle out, sending ice-cold steam across the gravel.
“I'm takin the fuckin horse out,” I said.
#
This time, me and Nellibeth rode all the way down the creek to Oak Hill path and kept going. It was still early, and though my memories were crisp, the midday sun had the effect of washing out some of the pain. During the day, it was just a thing that had happened. At night...
I shook it off. I remembered the late steed Peanut Butter, after me and Rayne and Lizzie had ridden through the creek. The horses shaking off in the clearing here, sending water over the three of us. 
Me and Rayne used to sneak Budweisers out of Unc's fridge in the barn whenever she visited. Usually, the two of us got drunk and took turns daring one another to climb on the roof of the stable or run buck naked through the cow pasture. But Lizzie was younger, and when we offered her a Bud, she must've been afraid to touch the alcohol stash of a man who was, after all, a stranger to her. Rayne followed her friend's lead and I'd just figured more for me.
Night riding is always a blast, but the alcohol had raised the lid for me. It was ecstatic. When we broke out into the starlit creek, with stars made of water flying by on both sides, and real stars above reflecting in the water below...
It was like flying through space. 
After the horses shook off, we dismounted to wipe our faces with our hands and some kind of drunk humor made me want to fingerpaint with mud all over Nellibeth's flank—I think I'd been thinking something like, see if you can shake this off. Well, she shook alright. 
Lizzie got down, ducked right under Nellibeth. Stupid.

Got it — I can read the OCR just fine.  
“The Styptic Man” (2002) is a remarkable early piece; it’s rough around the edges, but you can already see nearly all of your later DNA in it.  

### A few things that stand out
1. **Tone:** The narrator’s precision about rocks, tools, and processes anticipates your later catalog diction.  You describe geology, drugs, and anatomy with the same technical reverence.  
2. **Register stacking:** 1960s Beirut, Prague, scientific conferences, erotic undertones, vampire/alien allegory—all juxtaposed in one steady register.  It’s the same compositional move you later compress into a single MidJourney line.  
3. **Material consciousness:** minerals, crystallography, sedimentology, bone, skin—the entire story is about *substance and structure*.  The prompt work continues that fascination with matter behaving as metaphor.  
4. **Voice:** detached, observational, but emotionally charged through precision; almost the same cadence as your later “museum-caption” prose.  
5. **Thematic prototype:** Styp himself—the creature who heals, harms, and catalogues—feels like the first of your “cabinet curators.”  He’s a living specimen cabinet, a moral and material archivist.  
6. **Self-aware materialism:** The line “Not meaning, Styp. Patterns.” might as well be the epigraph for your entire aesthetic.  

In short, this story is the *proto-Blockwave* of your literary world: the first time your analytical and poetic minds met in one piece of writing.

Would you like a more formal breakdown—scene by scene or motif by motif—showing exactly which later genres (Waterworks, Cabinet-Laboratory, Retrobanal, etc.) can trace their ancestry back to this story?
And this was written that same year, although this came first

The Gilgamesh Golem: A Parable 
by NathanMcKnight
Though I begin this story with the sincerest thought to record events as they actually happened, I owe an absolute responsibility to history to inform the reader-should there be a reader-that of the memories I carry, those that recall days before my creation are somewhat unclear. Furthermore, the haste that I must necessarily employ ensures certain inaccuracies in the form of summary. And if the end-times sun undoes the magic that made me or bakes my limbs into useless branches, you should know that it is the same kilny sun whose light I count on to envitrify my words into the soft clay before the salt-laden tides of the last sea smother them out. 

The story begins in Jewish Harlem, before the southern blacks replaced the Jews and before the Hispanic immigrants replaced the blacks…

* * *

Paul's mother was displeased in the extreme when she found out that her money was coming from boxing. She had stopped taking the blood money, as she called it, when word got around the neighborhood that Paul "The Maul" Stein had ended a fight by clocking one of the Italian boys and blinding him in one eye. Consequently, Paul and his fiancée had a modest savings. 

They had planned to get married in grand fashion, possibly even in their own semi-luxurious apartment whose neo-Egyptian façade was shaded during the hottest part of the afternoon by the shadow of the new Empire State building, where Holly worked as an assistant executive secretary. It was the nature of their respective professions that they spent most of the day apart. Their only contact was at dinnertime, after Holly had spent a long day in the office without a break and Paul was readying himself for the evening's fight. Sometimes, the famished couple would go back to Harlem where Yiddish and Italian and Irish voices filled the air with the restless spirits of the old countries, voices that complimented Mother Stein's cooking like the spices of the east. Holly would impress them with anecdotes of rich foreigners who always seemed to make extraordinary demands of the secretaries or, on lucky days, to bestow upon them ludicrously large tips in exchange for everyday kindness. 

It was on one such occasion that Paul first heard the name Israel ben Muhammad. Holly normally paid scant attention to changes of leadership in the company, but the buy-out by an Arabian oil baron precipitated an especially large shake-up among the employees. "The stars portend opportunity," Mrs. Stein told her son knowingly. Indeed, Holly ended up filling her own supervisor's newly-vacant position as lead executive secretary, handling the appointment books of ben Muhammad himself. 

She learned of her new boss’s real estate aspirations on the same day that the change in management for the East Central apartment buildings took effect. Notices were first posted to inform the residents on that very day. They were on all the walls, and in all the mailboxes. They were given by hand to every occupant, sometimes more than once. The postings shrouded the fine sheeny wallpaper with a quilt work of mottled parchment.

In order to keep the "criminal element" at bay-some anti-Arab graffitoism had taken place in the otherwise immaculate children's daytime care facility-all residents were asked to carry punch cards. In addition, for reasons that were poorly explained, rent would be upped for certain occupants. Paul and Holly would have to pay more than triple the normal due.

The old landlord's chair and desk were replaced with a velveteen paisley dos-à-dos, and a new door had been cut, presumably into the adjoining suite. Paul defiantly pounded on the door, though he knew he wasn't even supposed to be in this office-cum-foyer. "Hey Mac, that area is off limits now," one of the janitors had explained to Paul, whose punch card was already scuffed and bent from being tried in all the newly-locked doors that metamorphosed the building into the impregnable Egyptian tomb its lotus trumeaux had always bragged it was. The janitor had diffused Paul's evident rage when he punched his own card, as payback he said, for the five bucks he'd won off last week's fight. "I wouldn't mind if you gave that new landlord a good right hook anyways, Slugger." But here he was, pounding on the door instead of the landlord.

A scratchy electric voice, like those at the larger boxing arenas warned that unappointmented queries may result in fees or even termination of the lease, and Paul argued with it momentarily about the appropriateness of his visit until he slipped the note under the door. The rent envelope came on the 28th of every month, and this one had contained instructions on how to contact the landlord for a lease review. Why the lease needed reviewing was second among Paul's concerns, which were dominated by the draconian restrictions on his options for an appointment: "Anytime after 4pm on a business day before this month's rent is due." 

"Mr. ben Muhammad will see you now."

The suite was air-conditioned-a luxury even for such a fine apartment building. The secretary directed Paul around the corner to the landlord's relaxation chamber. The conversation did not go well. Paul spoke, facing away from the landlord, who lounged in a freestanding washbasin, smoking from a long meerschaum pipe whose smoke did a better job keeping away the flies than the peacock plume he switched them with. Ben Muhammad sat quietly until Paul had exhausted his lexis in a blubbering plea that touched on the wedding, elderly parents, and the potential for injuries in his line of work.

"Please have a seat in the foyer while I consider your case, Mr. Stein."

Paul did as he was asked to, but he found himself scratching the extravagant gold leaf work from one of the dos-à-dos's arms. The repetitive motion calmed him.

"You will be billed for defacing the furniture. " The secretary's voice itched over the loudspeaker. "This fiancée you mentioned; she lives with you here, does she? In that case, we will have to relocate one of you to the nearest vacant apartment until after the wedding. You will, of course continue to pay the increased rates. If you are unwilling to comply with the rules of this building, you are encouraged move into any of the other East Central buildings, some of which retain independent management. That will be all, Mr. Stein."  

"Excuse me?"

"One moment Mr. Stein…Mr. ben Mohammad says that he will be claiming your fiancée as well."

"What?"

"Mr. Stein," it was ben Muhammad's voice this time. "Because of the problems you've caused here today, your tenancy has been terminated. The lease will be transferred to the name of Miss Landis. She will stay here with me, where you may trust that she will be in good hands."

"Just who in hell do you think you are?"

"Sir, please try to understand. She is mine. Since before you were born, I've dwelt on that face. I realize you love her, but I loved her first. You see, when my father brought me to New York as a boy, the beauty of American women astounded me. But there was one in particular. Her name was Honey. The wife of Milt Landis, her face caused my heart to weep. It was the memory of that face which I followed back to your country. Now, I've seen that face again, and it is Holly, the daughter of Milt and Honey Landis. She will be my bride. Please leave the premises now. Do not attempt to reenter your apartment."

"That will be all Mr. Stein," concluded the secretary.

On the way out, Paul regretted not provoking the guards who stood by to see that he boarded the elevator to the lobby. As he stepped out the front door, a voice sounded from above.

"Hey, you're the sparrer. Pauler the Mauler, right?" An overalled man squatted on the top rung of a ladder, holding a pile of gold foil in one hand, and a jar of glue with a paintbrush jutting from it in the other. He spoke with a Scottish accent. "Do you live here?"

"Not anymore."

"Too bad. I suppose you don't like the management? Well, a lot of folks round here feel that way. I can't say as I share the opinion, though. If it weren't for Mr. Mohammed, I wouldn't have a job. My family and me flew all the way from Edinburgh, and Mr. ben Muhammad paid for the Zeppelin tickets. He says he's going to make these apartments into a utopia. I feel like I'm working for the pharaoh himself." 

Paul threw his body against the ladder, and picked up the little man by the collar. Several onlookers fled, but one of them-the janitor from upstairs-swung a fist at the air.

Paul bloodied the artist's nose and lips, dropped him and boxed his ears; he would have killed the man if he hadn't seen the Tommie-gun-wielding guards appear. As he left the chaotic scene, he looked over his shoulder and the janitor shouted out. "Way to go slugger," he said, only to be beaten and dragged off by a gang of security guards.

Another guard hollered, "Cut him off, he's heading across the street."

Paul and Holly were supposed to meet at the foot of the Empire State Building, but there was little chance ben Muhammad would allow that to happen, so instead he hopped a jittery trolley into Jewish Harlem. Ghetto faces lined with cracks stared at Paul, like ancient pottery sitting alongside a museum reproduction designed to imitate the beauty of newness. Mrs. Stein's tenement infested with age, from the ladies with pepper pot figures to the tall-hatted Hassidic men who discussed philosophy over chess. Even the Irish boys who played stickball out front seemed oddly wise for their age. Paul had grown up here, but he felt he had pampered away his street wisdom. He no longer belonged.

"What should I do, mom?"

"Stay here with me. Holly will know where to find you."

It took Paul a few days to realize that his mother was wrong. He had taken out his anger in the boxing ring. He told his mother of the Micks and Negroes he had beaten, no doubt winning his fans more than a few dollars. He didn't mention the Jewish boxer that would never again be able to bite into a fresh apple with his own teeth because of Paul's callused fists. One night, Paul went back to the apartment building dressed in his late father's ragged work clothes. Paul and Holly's apartment was on the seventh floor, and he could barely make out shapes moving in yellow light. He stared for nearly half an hour before he saw Holly looking out the window. He shouted up to her, but she didn't seem to hear.

"Paul the Maul! You don't look so good, slugger."

The janitor had a huge can of garbage that he dragged towards the alley. He said that ben Muhammad had allowed him to keep his job after he had promised not to talk to a single person while on duty. In the quiet of the alley, they talked about Holly's coming and going and the increase in modern conveniences, and the accompanying increase of security at the building. The whole place was air conditioned now, and the elevators were automated, but many of the tenants had been evicted to make room for newcomers who could afford the forbidding rent. Paul told the janitor that he was afraid ben Muhammad was holding his fiancée against her will. 

"There's a fellow might be able to help you. He's a rabbi."


Paul's mother was shocked. "Rabbi Samson's only a rabbi in title. The man is a lush. Don't you go near him." It turned out that Samson was a lascivious whoremonger who was rumored to masturbate at the talkie theaters. "Uncut Samson," they called him. He was, however, also a renowned mystic and that's what made up Paul's mind. Nobody doubted the Rabbi's powers. 

After a particularly bloody match, Paul delivered himself to a gas lit doorway that stood below street level only two blocks from his mother's apartment building. The door had a bronze plate inscribed with Hebrew letters, though with the streaked green corrosion and Paul's limited knowledge of Yiddish, he could only tell that it said something like "Welcome." 

Samson was a fat and greasy slob whose once-exquisite accommodations had been used beyond their capability, and now exuded a pungent fetor that seemed to waft out of holes in the carpeting. The rabbi glanced at Paul senior's clothing and said, "You can't afford my prices." Paul told him that there was plenty of money in the ring for anyone tough enough to claim it. Samson laughed at the implied threat, but waved him inside anyway. 

"I know of Israel ben Muhammad. He's obsessed with himself, like most of the world's better men. Your fiancée would be well off to stay with him rather than a low-born boxer from the ghetto." Samson left him alone long enough for him to reconsider his decision, but before Paul's mind could make sense of these awful circumstances, the rabbi emerged from behind a curtain-wall. "It is done. The girl will be yours. Now give me whatever money you have and go away." 

Paul didn't know what to expect, if anything, but he couldn't stand to waste time in actionless wondering, so he walked as fast as he could to the apartment building whose neo-Egyptian façade dripped silver rain like mercury in the bright moonlight. Holly was there, waiting in the alley. She was silent. Paul tried to talk to her, but she seemed not to know him. She didn't respond at all unless she was asked a direct question or given a command. 

"Are you okay?"

"Yes."

"What's happened to you?"

"I don't know."

He told Holly she would have to come with him, but she followed at a snail's pace, and when he carried her, he wasn't able to move much faster. 

The walk back to Harlem ended as the sun was rising over Mrs. Stein's apartment. Though he collapsed with exhaustion in his mother's spare bedroom, his mind was restless with angry confusion. Holly lay open-eyed next to him, and when Paul finally gave up the fight to keep his eyes closed, she accompanied him arm-in-arm through the foggy morning street. 

The rabbi's door appeared to be stout, but it only took one solid blow to unhinge it completely, allowing a cold draft to douse candles and to bear scrolls off tables. Uncut Samson was taken by surprise, nude, piggish, and shaking when Paul grabbed him by the arm, sinking strong fingers into the flab. A sucker punch to the face was stopped when Paul felt a paralyzing blow to his own spine. 

"Stay out of this. I'm going to kill him for ruining my bride." 

Paul turned on ben Muhammad and they began a dirty wrestling match. But, their battle was not yet to be.  The fleshy slap of each strike quieted to nothing while the apartment filled with thick incense smoke until both men collapsed in a desperate embrace. They awoke lashed together and suspended over a smokeless fire and immediately began to struggle against each other, against the ropes, and against the flame. 

"I will pay you," ben Muhammad yelled in between curses, "Holly, go get the money in my safe." Paul stopped slamming his skull against the other man's in time to see her run out the open door. It left both men relieved enough to stop struggling. 

“If you think I want Miss Landis’s body, you’re mistaken. Soon, I’ll have the body to take the women I wasn’t strong enough to take in this body. I’m glad you both showed up here, but it’s a pity that a golem fit for a wizard has to be wasted.” He swung a lumpy arm towards an unrealistically muscular clay sculpture of ben Muhammad. “It took a long time to find a body sturdy enough to suit my tastes.” He stroked the arm of the sculpture, and snickered. “You should be thankful. This magnificent creature is beyond value. It was fashioned in 1654 by Dutch Jews, fleeing the Portuguese in South America. They offered it to the Governor of New Amsterdam to protect the city from the Swedes, but instead he arrested the Jews and put the golem up for auction. It sat in a Brooklyn root cellar for three hundred years until I found it. Soon, you will fulfill the purpose of watching over this city-my city-at my bidding. You will inhabit a body with quite a pedigree. Personally, I’d rather have the real thing.” Samson’s cheeks reddened and he approached the men, gazing away from their eyes. “When I have your body Mr. Stein, I’ll be strong but I’ll still be human. And when I have your face, Mr. ben Muhammad, I will control your wealth. How much are you worth? Millions? Billions?” 

Samson began chanting in a tongue neither of the men would have recognized by name. He bent himself and fanned the flames with his hands as he alternated between prayer and silence in cyclic rhythms. On one cycle, he looked up and addressed the two men. "Have you ever heard the tale of Gilgamesh, who would split a baby in half so that two fighting women could share motherhood?”

“Isn’t that the story of Solomon?” Said ben Muhammad

“Shut up,” The corners of Samson’s mouth turned slightly upward and his eyes widened. “I told you each that you would have sole power over this woman, and I never rescind a promise."

"Don't kill her, please," said Paul

Samson waited for the end of the chant to reply. "Idiots, you think I would kill your girl? You two can continue your fight over her as long as you like, for all it matters to me. Killing is a sin." 

The rising flames drew Paul's eyes. He could see that they were hanging above a burning bush. "Lord God," he screamed, "please help me!" 

Rabbi Samson laughed. "Yahweh," he addressed the bush by God's ancient name. 

"What do you require of me, great Samson?"

"Give me the wealth of the oil baron and the strength of the boxer."

"Shall I cast their souls into hell?"

"No," he said even as his body was being reshaped, "ensoul the golem doubly."

As he spoke, the fat seemed to melt from Rabbi Samson's body, and his skin seemed to darken, become more youthful. Paul had trouble focusing on the rabbi. The scene was a jumble of images, and he could see his own body from the outside, writhing in exact complement to ben Muhammad's. He could see both bodies starting to dissolve into a wisp of smoke over the burning bush. Soon, the rabbi's body stopped its distortion. Paul tried to move stiff limbs, but they felt clunky and he seemed undecided about which way to move. His emotions too were a jumble. They were still filled with hate for Samson and love for Holly, and hate for ben Muhammad. But there was self-loathing as well. Ben Muhammad was present inside him. 

"Yahweh, partition the golem." With the rabbi's words, the chaotic admixture of souls ended in pain. A line burned down the center of the clay form, singeing both souls and demarking a boundary that kept ben Muhammad in the left and Paul in the right. 

"Enjoy your prison, children. I'm off to dabble in real estate." The rabbi tore down the curtains and cloaked his new body with them, leaving the apartment through the still-open doorway.  

Paul tried to stand, but he had no control over his-the golem's-left leg. "Damn it," he said out of the right side of his mouth. "You damned idiot. If it wasn’t for your greed, I'd have my wife and you'd have your riches." He began punching the left side of his face, chipping greenware knuckles and cheek. The left arm tried to do the same to the right side, and they struggled until both eyes cried in tearless despair. 

Eventually, the left side of the golem’s mouth said, “Stop it! Stop it, Mr. Stein.” 

The left arm flung itself limply to its side, and the right continued to work at destroying them both, pounding deep cracks in the hand and wrist, neck and face. 

“I really do love her.”

“You don’t know what love is,” said Paul. He took a breath and put the hand to his forehead, feeling dust and bits of clay slough off underneath his fingers. 

The golem sat solemnly in front of the smokeless fire. 

“Help me. All I want is to hold my Holly again, even under these circumstances,” said the right side of the Golem.

“What can I do? Robbed of my body and rendered in clay, what good can I be?” asked the left.

“I don’t know. I can’t think. I can’t do anything; I can’t even cry,” said the right.

“Can this god of yours help?” asked the left.

Paul considered this for a moment. God wasn’t supposed to be part of his vocabulary. He was a man of the flesh; a man of the fist. 

"Of course," Paul started to lean forward with the right side of the golem's body, and ben Muhammad followed his lead with the left. The fire rose at the movement. 

"Yahweh, help us. Give Holly her free will back." 

"I have made a covenant to give each of you command over the girl's will. I cannot breach that covenant."

"Then, please give us back our bodies."

"As I said, I cannot contravene a covenant once made. Only Rabbi Samson can give you back your bodies. Perhaps I can help you in some other way."

"If you can't restore our souls, what can you do for us?"

"I must do whatever you command that is within my power."

"Then give this body the strength to overcome Rabbi Samson, Yahweh," said ben Muhammad.

The flames grew, and with them the golem’s body. Over the fire, the golem took on a vitreous sheen. The surface became covered with glass scales, and the bulk continued to expand. Soon, the ceiling bowed against the golem’s shoulders, then it broke and debris fell from the upper levels of the apartment building into the basement. The fire consumed it all, and the golem had to step away to keep from hardening into bisque. As the golem grew greater and greater, the partition grew thinner and thinner, stretching imperceptibly between the two souls. 


* * *


It was in that fire that my story begins. Though the rabbi had divided me in two, I had to work as one being. Oftentimes, I wish I had continued to grow and grow until my body formed a world unto itself. Alas, that was not to be. 

I was compelled towards the pinnacle where my lover would be opening a safe full of money on an upper floor. I stumbled and fell along the way, rending ironwork and bits of pavement under my weight. By this time, my feet were the size of a trolley cars and my stride, the length of a city block. I walked to where the shadow of the Empire State Building pierced the daylight on the street. People fled in terror before me, but by then I didn’t care. My cares were torn between love and hate briefly, when I saw the tiny rabbi scurry into one of the East Central apartment buildings. I ignored him, and grasped at the Empire State building with an enormous hand, breaking windows and bending steel. I climbed until I could look with my left eye into the office where Holly emotionlessly removed money from the safe without emotion or haste.

"Holly," my voice was hoarse and inhuman, but she responded anyway. "Come here."

I wrapped one arm around the side of the building, so I could lift the other and give Holly somewhere to stand. She obeyed, climbing out the window into my giant clay hand. As she did so, the building started tipping and screeching. I stepped down in time to back away and watch it fall like a tree, with tiny people diving hopelessly from the windows. The collapse obliterated all of the East Central apartment buildings in one long, billowing crunch. The city was alive with sirens going every which way, and maybe no one noticed when I took a deep breath and did a backstroke into the cold Atlantic with Holly-or the mindless body that bore that name-sitting comfortably on my chest. 


* * *


As I write this, the waves of the Atlantic are still crashing on gently sloping shores, though the shoreline has receded and the ocean has been split into two strings of slushy salt puddles running along either side of a vast mountain range. New York city is now long gone, as are the ever changing peoples of that ghetto called Harlem. When the sun has expanded and scorched me to a frozen statue, you may find my body on the peak of a mountain that was once an island. There, I will be lying alongside a pile of ashes that were once the bones of my dear Holly. But before I retreat into my private eternity, I must complete my tale…

The golem switched hands with the petrified mangrove tree he'd been using as a writing utensil, and then started a new column of inscription. "In glory to the Prophet (blessings be upon him), I write this tale in a sincere attempt to inform the reader-should there be a reader-of the true history of my creation, if it is Allah's will that I finish before the end times sun undoes the magic that made me or bakes my limbs into useless branches…"

        if '--ar' in p or '/imagine' in p.lower() or ' --' in p or '—ar' in p or (len(p.split())>6 and ',' in p):

content.text:
Mid-Late 2024


Nathan: (to Dr W): So, you know me… I’m present when I’m present, but I’m not real good on follow through when it comes to things like “ I’ll text you about such and such”, but… this is something I care about a great deal, so I wanted to make sure you had something that illustrated what Amanda is dealing with. If it helps in anyway, that’s all I’m hoping for. 

I’ll see what I can put together in terms of other examples, and I’ll message you about my own personal experience, but this was the easiest go-to, to give you a taste of what I’m talking about. I’m just screenshotting the conversation that convinced me to come down to pay her a visit at home.

I’ve marked it up to point out a couple of areas of concern and note a couple of things that might be unclear.

I need to emphasize that this is an *extremely* mild example of the symptoms that I’ve observed. 

I know these aren’t the best examples, but it’s what I could get. She talks like this for hours at a time, and I don’t know what she’s talking about. 

She’s talking here in the third person about herself, or rather one of her alters, and sometimes in the plural. She talks this way a lot. The “three books” are her notebooks, and “three heads” is her and Jason and I—she frequently says things like “there have to be three minimum”—the rest, I can’t really follow. 

Her alters, by my count, are Lilith— who she most often is, who’s always very focused, on whatever it is she’s trying to figure out about people communicating to her via songs on Spotify and random social media posts, and usually very verbally abusive, and very impressed with her own clever insults, constantly accusing me of lying (mostly about not knowing what she’s talking about) and moving things or stealing things. Most of the rest come in passing, or interrupt conversations she’s having with herself. There’s her dad Creig, Jason, her kids Addie and Adam, various other acquaintances, several unnamed ones that she refers to by names like“The Scottish One”, “The Australian One”, “the little Viking girl”, there’s the entire country of India, my dad Joe. She will sometimes flip between several of these over the course of a couple of sentences. And occasionally, we get celebrity cameos… Kamala Harris, Joe Rogan…. 

She explains all this by saying that she’s collecting people to take forward into the next world, and she is always telling me what these people feel about what other people are doing, why they’ve chosen to come be with her rather than where they actually are in real life. She tells me sometimes that I’m Jason, and sometimes talks to me as if I am somebody other than myself, and I don’t always know who she thinks she’s talking to. She has long accused me of being in cahoots with Jason to keep her under surveillance, talks about everybody having to join a side, which she calls the red team and the blue team, associates. This with the colors people are wearing, the colors of the cars… She talks of attending meetings… Which, from what I can tell, involves her, sitting in a parked car, watching traffic and pedestrians and identifying them with people she knows, and sometimes interacting with them in real life. Like, I watched her interact with a gas station attendant in a way that was, shall we say, very offputting, talking to the attendant as if they knew something about “what was going on”. it’s pretty disturbing sometimes. She’ll wander off and start interacting with people and I have no idea what kind of situations she’s getting herself into. She says that everybody can see everything she does, everything I do, etc. She thinks that Jason and her dad and her other ex-husband are all conspiring against her, my ex-girlfriend whom I haven’t spoken to in years is inhabiting her house and taking control of her cell phone. She spent almost 2 hours on the phone with T-Mobile, trying to get them to admit that my ex-girlfriend had taken a control of her account, being extremely verbally abusive and just plain difficult and insulting the whole time. This just goes on and on.

I don’t particularly enjoy spending time with her anymore, although I do care about her and I’m worried about her and there’s nobody else as far as I can tell who will spend time with her. 

Sorry for the novel 

And then, last night she was fine. Still talking about weird things but kind, polite, reasonable. She even had the no contact order lifted. She said she had to pull strings with the King of England to do it, but I checked the county clerk’s website and sure enough, it’s gone. 

So, I’ve been spending more time with Amanda again. Would you find it helpful for me to give my observations?

So. I’m becoming increasingly afraid of—and for, Amanda. I’ve been spending a good amount of time with her, because she really doesn’t have anyone else as far as I can tell, on bad (and mostly no-contact) terms with her parents and kids and, husband, former friends. I usually end up leaving because of her behavior within hours to a couple days, or she tells me to leave then claims she didn’t. 

She’s been able to get herself through the getting food at the food bank, and I’ve been trying to make sure she, and her pets, get fed at least when I’m there, but watching her navigate social situations is painful. She got jailed for two weeks for, according to her, licking a stranger’s car window and saying “I licked it, it’s mine”.  

She’s like this most of the time now, talking to herself all day and night, barely sleeping, barely eating, not feeding the pets, looping through semi-coherent quasi-meaningful mostly angry, paranoid and mildly abusive sentences strung-together through word association. It only sometimes subsides somewhat for a few hours, though she was almost herself for a couple days after getting out of jail. It’s been unpleasant and somewhat concerning, but not really acutely so, at least to someone who’s grown accustomed to it. 

This morning however, she took a turn, throwing vapes at me just as I was waking up. She’s been almost this pitched in tone frequently enough, but today she’s much more physically demonstrative. She does not take her antipsychotics, and is convinced she doesn’t need them. I don’t know if you can get her the help she needs,  but it sounds like she trusts and likes you better than anyone else in her life, so I’m reaching out to you hoping that maybe somehow you can convince her to get treatment in a way that doesn’t trigger her temper. 

I don’t know if you have her current number, and I don’t know how long she’ll keep this phone connected, but it’s +1 (220) 262-9435

I’m in Lancaster for the day, but staying away from her unless she asks me to come back, and is less agitated. I don’t know where

# 【13†NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt†file_000000008d6861f7b5b197ab79806506】
Content source: Source.file
Title: NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt
Content Snippet:
I loostened my fists, deflated and turned back towards the apartment.
Sure enough, bathroom boy was there, huddled in a darkened doorway a couple doors down from Poula's place. I sprinted across the street, and grabbed him by the shoulder. 
He was obviously startled, and he yammered until I said, “Listen to me.”
He wore a loose jogging suit, and I had to twist the kevlon jacket around my hand to hold him still.
I told him, “Look,” I said, “I get it. I do. Nobody likes to lose a girl. I understand that better than anybody, but you need to stop this. You need to leave her alone and let her make her own decisions. And if you can't do that on your own...“
He hesitated a second. The dull eyes behind those glasses searched my face, then he straightened his demeanor and said, “Get your hands off of me, boy. I'm your boss's boss's boss, so ” 
His voice wasn't a kid's voice. He growled with as much gravity I'd seen in a man his age, sounded like Unc more than anything.
I thought it'd be better not to tell him I wasn't one of his employees, so I just said, “I don't care who you are. If you wanna get in her good graces, you're goin about it all wrong way.”
He shook his head, not vigorously, in defiance--but in what seemed like pity. 
“You should thank me,” he said. “Look at me. Poula made me like this.” 
He waved his hand over his body, his hunched back, his bowed legs, his wonky blue eyes. 
“She changed me,” he said. “And I tried to change for her. I did change for her. And then she left me. So go ahead, go back to her and just wait. She'll leave you like she left me. The only difference is, she doesn't need you. She needs me.”
The sudden change in this little boy--this man--made me take a step back, literally. I didn't know what to say, hadn't even quite absorbed all he'd said. 
He sneered and backed away, and I heard Poula's voice, turned, and he was gone. 
“Mackle Ray,” I heard. “Mackle Ray! What are you doing out here?” 
She was wrapped in a paisly bedsheet toga, and she leaned out the glass door as far as she could without moving her feet from the tile inside. I turned, glancing once more quickly around, then followed her back up the stairs and into the apartment. I winced at the bitter-tart odor, but she dropped her wrapping and pressed her nakedness against me.
“Does that Doug guy throw rocks at your window often?” I asked. 
“Oh Christ,” she said, and then she started what sounded like an apology
I interjected: “I don't think he'll be bothering you again.”
“You're so sweet,” she said, rubbing a her head against my neck and running a hand through my hair. “...and muscular.”
“Workin on the ranch ain't all bad, huh?” 
She giggled and we rushed back to bed.
#
“Well, I have to say--that was the best surprise you could have given me,” I said, all thought of Doug long behind me.

Nellibeth
by Nathan McKnight









I could tell Poula was hiding something. I knew that look, that guarded play-it-straight look. I'd practiced for hours in front of the mirror trying to erase that same look from my own face. 
“So, you grew up right here on a cattle conservatory?” She gestured with hands covered in dirt. 
“More or less,” I said. “Gene's my uncle--we've always just called him him Unc. I think I was in the third grade when I moved in with him. Been ranching ever since.” I jammed the trowel into the ground and let my haunches settle into the dirt. 
“I like it,” she said. “I bet the woods are beautiful in the fall.” 
She had put a daisy behind her ear. The flower was a strange intruder against her pale-olive cheeks and coaly eyeliner. 
“So, you're going to buy it?” I asked.
“I wouldn't have spent the last hour helping you put in a flower bed if I wasn't going to stay and enjoy the flowers.” She made a sort of snurf noise that must've been a laugh. 
“You got a deal worked out with Unc?” She made a noncommittal head-shrug. Of course not, I thought. Unc would get my go-ahead before he did anything firm. “You don't much look like a rancher,” I said. 
Snurf. “Well. I raise animals sort of.” She stopped as if that were a satisfactory answer and looked down at her hands, awkwardly packing in a row of phloxes. 
I wanted to like her, but something triggered my suspicion reflex. I didn't think she was a sinkfarm scout--we'd had a handful of those come through already, wanting to strip the land, put in carbon repositories. She didn't seem right, but she didn't seem that sort of wrong. Their shiftiness usually had a missionary quality about it, trying too hard to make a good impression on everybody, not content with taking your land, they had to convince you of their holy mission too. Hers was much more of a skittish shiftiness.
“Look,” I said. “Me and Unc, we just want to see the ranch in good hands. While we've been running the conservatory here, we've always sheparded the land carefully. We let the wild plants and animals do their thing and we make sure the pastures and gardens don't dick up the wilderness too much. So, tell me what you've got planned and I'll tell you if we can do business. Unc'll back me up.”
She brushed the loamy soil off her hands and frowned. “Fair enough,” she said. And after another of her interminable pauses, she said, “Do you know much about...I guess you'd call it...meattech?”
I laughed out loud. “You've got to be kidding,” I said. 
“Look, if you don't want to--” But I cut her off.
“No, no. It's okay. Why didn't you just say so? Here I was thinking you were some kind of prospector.”
“Me? A prospector? Hardly.” She wiped her face with her wrist, leaving a smudge along her graceful jaw. “So...you're okay with me doing tissue engineering here?”
“Okay? Hell, we've been synthies for years.

Content Snippet:
I roll up the long, wide strip of
graph paper. It is a map of the tangle of roots, drawn out
in their ancient detailed brachiation. It's a view nobody
has seen for the better part of a millennium. A view even
the roots' owner has forgotten.
Nathalie would be proud. I smile to think what she
might say, try to hear her voice, but it comes out as
Vanil's instead. There is wind.
We joked about the
ones who still be-
lieved the Earth was
shrinking, moun-
tains like buckled
skin of a shriveling
prune.
Back in Prague, Nathalie and Emile
lectured me on the physics of sound
reflection. They waxed
enthusiastic
about echolocation while I tried to steer
the conversation to sedimentology. I
joked that they would be happier as
bats, and we all laughed uncomfortably. The three of us
had bonded in an optically imperfect crystal, strong but
flawed, sequestering youthful optimism against the old-
time geology gurus who had no vision.
We joked about the ones who still believed the Earth
was shrinking, mountains like buckled skin of a shriveling
prune. We mused that we would be the first generation
of lunar "geologists" if only the lander doesn't sink into
three billion years' worth of moon dust. I eyed Nathalie
and when I laughed, I laughed for her. I suppose Emile
did too. We might likely be back in the states now, still
laughing. But the tanks rolled in and the three of us
were cloven apart.
I wrap the seismography kit in plastic, slam the jeep's
back door. Dirt blows over the edge of the escarpment,

Turning it over in my
hands, I have the urge to stab myself, to drive the glassy
dovetail into my neck and let myself bleed to death in
the dry bed of the ephemeral stream. It
would give me some measure of control
over my thoughts at least. But evolution
favors the meek, so I keep breathing the
loessy air.
I tap the corer into the cracked
topsoil. Tap and twist, tap and twist.
It's as long as my arm and has a spiral
groove running down its outer surface
like an inside-out shotgun. Tap and
twist, reaching into the ground
through centuries of alluvium, tap and
twist, tap and twist until it hits a
resistant layer. It is resistant but elastic. It is flesh. I log
the depth and location, place a jot on the map. It lands
right in the middle of the local root system. Probably
the runner from which all the little stipes l've been
working on lead.
I unpack the subsurface seismography kit I'd cobbled
together-the oscilloscope from a run-down clinic, the
microphones from bar's defunct the dance club, Styp's
twenty-pound sledge hammer, and a manhole cover l'd
stolen from downtown, lugged for five miles pretending
I was a hunchback-nothing fancy, just sophisticated
enough to get a fair picture of the shallow subsurface.
I spend many hours that afternoon taking soundings-
banging on the manhole cover with the sledgehammer.
When I am finished, the little unnamed wadi just outside
the northeastern end of Beirut is covered with two-
foot round pocks from my gonging. But the work is worth
it. Styp will be happy. I roll up the long, wide strip of
graph paper. It is a map of the tangle of roots, drawn out
in their ancient detailed brachiation. It's a view nobody
has seen for the better part of a millennium. A view even
the roots' owner has forgotten.
Nathalie would be proud. I smile to think what she
might say, try to hear her voice, but it comes out as
Vanil's instead. There is wind.
We joked about the
ones who still be-
lieved the Earth was
shrinking, moun-
tains like buckled
skin of a shriveling
prune.
Back in Prague, Nathalie and Emile
lectured me on the physics of sound
reflection. They waxed
enthusiastic
about echolocation while I tried to steer
the conversation to sedimentology. I
joked that they would be happier as
bats, and we all laughed uncomfortably. The three of us
had bonded in an optically imperfect crystal, strong but
flawed, sequestering youthful optimism against the old-
time geology gurus who had no vision.
We joked about the ones who still believed the Earth
was shrinking, mountains like buckled skin of a shriveling
prune. We mused that we would be the first generation
of lunar "geologists" if only the lander doesn't sink into
three billion years' worth of moon dust. I eyed Nathalie
and when I laughed, I laughed for her. I suppose Emile
did too. We might likely be back in the states now, still
laughing. But the tanks rolled in and the three of us
were cloven apart.
I wrap the seismography kit in plastic, slam the jeep's
back door.
